en: The Path of Discrimination 2:
The Chapter on the Coupling 2.7.
The Discourse on the Wheel of Dhamma
2.7.1. Chapter on Truths (Saccavāra) At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Bārāṇasī … [as before] … and thus the Venerable Koṇḍañña acquired the name “Koṇḍañña who has attained realization.”
“‘This is the noble truth of suffering’: regarding these things unheard of before, vision arose, knowledge arose, wisdom arose, true insight arose, and light arose.
When it is said that ‘vision arose,’ in what sense?”
“Knowledge arose”—
in what sense?
“Wisdom arose”— in what sense?
In what sense?
"True knowledge arose"—
in what sense?
"Light arose"—
in what sense?
"The eye arose"— in that sense.
"Knowledge arose" means in the sense of seeing; "knowledge arose" means in the sense of having known.
"Wisdom arose" means in the sense of understanding.
"True knowledge arose" means—
In the sense of penetration.
"Light arose"—
in the sense of radiance.
The eye is the phenomenon; its meaning is the sense of seeing.
Knowledge is the phenomenon; its meaning is the sense of knowing.
Wisdom is the phenomenon; its meaning is the sense of understanding.
Knowledge is the phenomenon; its meaning is penetration.
Light is the phenomenon; its meaning is radiance.

These five phenomena and five meanings have suffering as their basis, the truths as their basis, the truths as their object, the truths as their domain, and are comprised within the truths, included within the truths, arisen from the truths, established in the truths, and grounded in the truths.
In what sense is it the "Wheel of Dhamma" (Dhammacakka)?
It is the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets the Dhamma in motion and it is a wheel; it is the Wheel of Dhamma because it is a wheel and it sets the Dhamma in motion.
It sets in motion by means of the Dhamma; thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
It sets in motion through the practice of the Dhamma; thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
It sets in motion while established in the Dhamma; thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
One who, being established in the Dhamma, sets it in motion—it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
One who, establishing others in the Dhamma, sets it in motion—it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
One who has attained mastery over the Dhamma sets it in motion—it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
It is called the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets in motion while bringing mastery over the Dhamma;
it is called the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets in motion having reached perfection in the Dhamma;
it is called the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets in motion while leading others to perfection in the Dhamma.
It is called the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets in motion [the teaching] having attained fearlessness regarding the Dhamma;
it is called the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets in motion [the teaching] while instilling fearlessness regarding the Dhamma;
it is called the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets in motion [the teaching] while honoring the Dhamma.
It is called the Wheel of Dhamma because it is set in motion by one who holds the Dhamma in high esteem; it is called the Wheel of Dhamma because it is set in motion by one who honors the Dhamma;
it is called the Wheel of Dhamma because it is set in motion by one who venerates the Dhamma.

One who honors the Dhamma sets it in motion—it is the Wheel of the Dhamma. One who raises the banner of the Dhamma sets it in motion—it is the Wheel of the Dhamma. One who raises the standard of the Dhamma sets it in motion—it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
It is called the Wheel of Dhamma because it proceeds with the Dhamma as its sovereign.
Furthermore, that Wheel of Dhamma is irreversible by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world—thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
The faculty of faith is the Dhamma; it proceeds with that Dhamma—thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
The faculty of energy is a phenomenon; it sets that phenomenon in motion—thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
The faculty of mindfulness is a phenomenon; it sets that phenomenon in motion—thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
The faculty of concentration is a phenomenon; it sets that phenomenon in motion—thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
The faculty of wisdom is a Dhamma; because it sets that Dhamma in motion, it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
The power of faith is a Dhamma; because it sets that Dhamma in motion, it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
The power of energy is a Dhamma; because it sets that Dhamma in motion, it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
The power of mindfulness is Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
The power of concentration is Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
The power of wisdom is Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
The enlightenment factor of mindfulness is a state; it sets that state in motion—thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
The enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena is a state; it sets that state in motion—thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
The enlightenment factor of energy is a state; it sets that state in motion—thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
The enlightenment factor of rapture is a Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion—thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
The enlightenment factor of tranquility is a Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion—thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
The enlightenment factor of concentration is a Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion—thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
The factor of enlightenment that is equanimity is a state; because it sets that state in motion, it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
Right view is a state; because it sets that state in motion, it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
Right intention is a state; because it sets that state in motion, it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
Right speech is Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
Right action is Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
Right livelihood is Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
Right effort is the Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion—thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
Right mindfulness is the Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion—thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
Right concentration is the Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion—thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
A state is a faculty in the sense of predominance; because it sets that state in motion, it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
A state is a power in the sense of unshakability; because it sets that state in motion, it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
A state is an enlightenment factor in the sense of leading out; because it sets that state in motion, it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
In the sense of being the cause, the Dhamma is the Path; it sets that Dhamma in motion—thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma (Dhammacakka).
In the sense of establishing, the Dhamma is the Foundations of Mindfulness; it sets that Dhamma in motion—thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
In the sense of striving, the Dhamma is the Right Exertions; it sets that Dhamma in motion—thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
In the sense of success, the bases for spiritual power (*iddhipāda*) are the Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma (*dhammacakka*).
In the sense of suchness, the truths (*sacca*) are the Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
In the sense of non-distraction, serenity (*samatha*) is the Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
In the sense of contemplation, insight is the Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
In the sense of having a single flavor, serenity and insight are the Dhamma; they set that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
In the sense of non-excess, the yoke-pair is the Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
Purification of virtue in the sense of restraint is the Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma (*dhammacakka*).
Purification of mind in the sense of non-distraction is the Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
Purification of view in the sense of seeing is the Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
The state that is liberation in the sense of being released is the Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion—thus, the Wheel of Dhamma.
The state that is true knowledge in the sense of penetration is the Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion—thus, the Wheel of Dhamma.
The state that is deliverance in the sense of relinquishment is the Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion—thus, the Wheel of Dhamma.
Knowledge of destruction in the sense of eradication is a Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma (Dhammacakka).
Knowledge of non-arising in the sense of subsiding is a Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
Zeal in the sense of being the root is a Dhamma; it sets that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
Attention is a *dhamma* in the sense of origination; it sets that *dhamma* in motion, thus it is the Wheel of *Dhamma*.
Contact is a *dhamma* in the sense of convergence; it sets that *dhamma* in motion, thus it is the Wheel of *Dhamma*.
Feeling is a *dhamma* in the sense of meeting together; it sets that *dhamma* in motion, thus it is the Wheel of *Dhamma*.
Concentration is the Dhamma in the sense of being foremost; it sets that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
Mindfulness is the Dhamma in the sense of being the dominant influence; it sets that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
Wisdom is the Dhamma in the sense of being supreme; it sets that Dhamma in motion, thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
The Dhamma is the "wheel of the Dhamma" (*dhammacakka*) in the sense that it sets in motion that Dhamma which has liberation as its essence.
The Dhamma is the "wheel of the Dhamma" in the sense that it sets in motion that Dhamma which is Nibbāna—the plunge into the Deathless—in the sense of being the ultimate goal.
"This Noble Truth of Suffering must be fully understood," and so on...
"Fully understood": regarding these previously unheard-of phenomena, vision arose … down to … light arose.
"Vision arose" means:
In what sense...
"light arose"—
in what sense?
“The eye arose” means in the sense of seeing … “light arose” means … [as above] … [end of formula].
In the sense of illumination.
The eye is the phenomenon (dhamma); the meaning is seeing.
… [and so on] … Light is the phenomenon; the meaning is illumination.

These five states and five meanings have suffering as their basis, the truths as their basis, the truths as their object, the truths as their domain; they are comprised by the truths, included within the truths, arisen from the truths, established in the truths, and grounded in the truths.
In what sense is it the "Wheel of Dhamma" (*dhammacakka*)?
It is the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets the Dhamma in motion and is itself a wheel.
It sets in motion both the wheel and the Dhamma—thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka). It sets in motion by means of the Dhamma—thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
It sets in motion through the practice of the Dhamma—thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
It is called the Wheel of Dhamma because it is set in motion by one established in the Dhamma.
It is called the Wheel of Dhamma because it is set in motion by one firmly grounded in the Dhamma...
[and so on] ...Nibbāna, which plunges into the Deathless, is "Dhamma" in the sense of being the ultimate goal; it is called the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets that Dhamma in motion.
“‘This is the noble truth of the origin of suffering’—thus, regarding things unheard of before, there arose in me the eye ...
the light ...
‘But this noble truth of the origin of suffering is to be abandoned’ ... [and so on].
“Abandoned”: regarding phenomena unheard of before, vision arose … [and so on] … light arose.
“Vision arose”—this is how it was said.
In what sense...
"light arose"—
in what sense?
"The eye arose" means in the sense of seeing ... [and so on] ...
"light arose" means:
In the sense of illumination:
the eye is the phenomenon (dhamma), while seeing is the meaning (attha) … pe … light is the phenomenon, while illumination is the meaning.
These five states and five meanings have origination as their basis,
have the truths as their basis … [and so on] … have cessation as their basis,

have the truths as their basis … [and so on] … have the path as their basis, have the truths as their basis; they have the truths as their object, have the truths as their domain, are comprised within the truths, are included within the truths, have arisen from the truths, are established in the truths, and are grounded in the truths.
In what sense is it the "Wheel of Dhamma" (dhammacakka)?
It is the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets the Dhamma in motion and is itself a wheel. It is the Wheel of Dhamma because it is a wheel and sets the Dhamma in motion.
It sets rolling in accordance with the Dhamma; thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
It sets rolling through conduct in accordance with the Dhamma; thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
It sets rolling while established in the Dhamma; thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
It sets in motion what is established in the Dhamma; thus it is the "Wheel of the Dhamma" (*dhammacakka*).
…pe… Nibbāna, which plunges into the Deathless, is the Dhamma in the sense of the ultimate goal; it sets in motion that Dhamma; thus it is the "Wheel of the Dhamma. 2.7.2.
Section on the Foundations of Mindfulness (*Satipaṭṭhānavāra*)
“‘This is contemplation of the body in the body,’ monks— regarding these things unheard of before, vision arose in me … light arose in me.
Moreover, ‘this contemplation of the body in the body is to be developed,’ monks …”
"‘It has been developed,’ monks— regarding these states unheard of by me before—
vision arose … light arose.
This is regarding feelings …" [and so on].
"This is the contemplation of mind...
this is the contemplation of phenomena in phenomena"—thus, monks, regarding these things unheard of before, there arose in me the eye...
the light.
"Furthermore, monks, regarding this contemplation of phenomena in phenomena:
'It is to be developed,' thus, monks, in regard to things unheard of before, there arose in me vision... light."
“‘This is contemplation of the body in the body’—thus, regarding things unheard before, there arose the eye ...
the light ...
‘And this contemplation of the body in the body is to be developed’ ... [and so on].
"Developed": regarding these previously unheard-of phenomena, vision arose … [and so on] … light arose.
"Vision arose"—this is what it means.
In what sense...
“light arose”—
in what sense?
“The eye arose” means in the sense of seeing … “light arose” means … [as above] … [end of formula].
In the sense of illumination.
The eye is the phenomenon (dhamma); the meaning is seeing.
…pe… Light is the phenomenon; the meaning is illumination.
These five states and five meanings have the body as their basis, have the foundations of mindfulness as their basis … [and so on] … have feelings as their basis,
have the foundations of mindfulness as their basis … have the mind as their basis,
have the foundations of mindfulness as their basis.

They have the Dhamma as their basis, the foundations of mindfulness as their basis, the foundations of mindfulness as their object, the foundations of mindfulness as their domain, they are comprised within the foundations of mindfulness, they are included in the foundations of mindfulness, they have arisen from the foundations of mindfulness, they are established in the foundations of mindfulness, and they are firmly grounded in the foundations of mindfulness.
In what sense is it called the "Wheel of Dhamma" (*dhammacakka*)?
It sets in motion the Dhamma and the wheel—thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhammacakka).
It sets in motion the wheel and the Dhamma—thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma. It sets in motion by means of the Dhamma—thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
It sets in motion by means of the practice of the Dhamma; thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
It sets in motion while established in the Dhamma; thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
It sets in motion while firmly grounded in the Dhamma; thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma... [and so on]...
Nibbāna, which is plunged into the Deathless, is the Dhamma in the sense of being the ultimate goal; one sets in motion that Dhamma, thus it is called the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka*).
2.7.3. Chapter on the Bases of Spiritual Power (*iddhipāda-vāra*):

“‘This is the basis of spiritual power endowed with concentration through desire and volitional formations of striving,’ monks, regarding these teachings unheard before, vision arose in me... [and so on] ...”
Light arose.

"This basis for psychic power, possessed of concentration through desire and volitional formations of striving, is to be developed"—thus, monks, regarding these states not heard before, vision arose in me ...
[and so on] ... "It has been developed"—thus, monks, regarding these states not heard before, vision arose in me ... [and so on].
Light arose.
This is concentration through energy …pe… this is concentration through the mind …pe…

“‘This is the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving’—thus, monks, regarding these states unheard of before, there arose in me the eye ...
the light.

‘Furthermore, this basis for psychic power endowed with concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving must be developed’—thus, monks, regarding these states unheard of before, there arose in me the eye ... the light.”
“‘It has been developed,’ monks— thus regarding these states unheard of before, vision arose in me … light arose.
“‘This is the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration through desire and volitional formations of striving’— regarding these states unheard of before, vision arose in me … light arose.”

Light arose … [as before] … “This basis for spiritual power (iddhipāda) consisting of concentration through desire and the volitional formations of striving is to be developed,” … [as before] … “It has been developed”—
regarding these things unheard of before, there arose in me vision, knowledge, wisdom, true knowledge, and light.
“Vision arose”—
in what sense? “Knowledge arose”— in what sense?
In what sense?
"Wisdom arose"—
in what sense?
"Knowledge arose"—
in what sense?
"Light arose"— in that sense.
In what sense?
"The eye arose" means in the sense of seeing.
"Knowledge arose"—
in the sense of what is known.
"Wisdom arose"— in the sense of understanding.
In the sense of understanding.
"True knowledge arose"—
in the sense of penetration.
"Light arose"—this is in the sense of radiance.
The eye is the phenomenon (dhamma); the meaning is the act of seeing.
Knowledge is the phenomenon; its meaning is that which is known.
Wisdom is the phenomenon; its meaning is the act of understanding.
Clear vision is the phenomenon; its meaning is penetration.
Light is the phenomenon; illumination is its meaning.

These five phenomena and five meanings have desire as their basis, the bases of psychic power as their basis, the bases of psychic power as their object, the bases of psychic power as their domain, are comprised within the bases of psychic power, are included in the bases of psychic power, have arisen from the bases of psychic power, abide in the bases of psychic power, and are firmly established in the bases of psychic power.
In what sense is it the "Wheel of Dhamma" (dhammacakka)?
It is the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets the Dhamma in motion and is itself a wheel. It is the Wheel of Dhamma because it is a wheel that sets the Dhamma in motion.
It sets rolling in accordance with the Dhamma; thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma. It sets rolling through practice in accordance with the Dhamma; thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
It sets rolling while established in the Dhamma; thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
One who, being established in the Dhamma, sets it in motion—it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
One who, establishing others in the Dhamma, sets it in motion—it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
One who, having attained mastery over the Dhamma, sets it in motion—it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
It is called the Wheel of Dhamma because it causes one to reach mastery over the Dhamma while setting it in motion;
it is called the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets in motion that which has reached perfection in the Dhamma;
it is called the Wheel of Dhamma because it sets in motion that which is causing others to reach perfection in the Dhamma... [and so on]...
One who honors the Dhamma sets it in motion—thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
One who raises the banner of Dhamma sets it in motion—thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma. One who raises the standard of Dhamma sets it in motion—thus it is the Wheel of Dhamma.
It is turned with the Dhamma as its sovereign; thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma (*dhammacakka*).
Furthermore, that Wheel of the Dhamma is irreversible by any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world; thus it is the Wheel of the Dhamma.
